title: CRD/ I
summary: A 1959 memo from Lt. Gen. Arthur G. Trudeau (Chief of Research and Development) to the Chief of Ordnance asks for a preliminary study of a proposed Army lunar outpost, with funding left to the Chief of Ordnance's discretion amid tight budgets. A draft requirement describes a 10-20 person manned military moon base for protecting US interests, moon-based surveillance and communications relay, exploration, scientific work, and possible military operations. It cites NSC/OCB space policy, the strategic race to get there first, and the need for a unified space command, with the base treated as a special project like the Manhattan Project.

nodes.title: A, GENERAL
A, GENERAL (intro)
nodes.summary: Project HORIZON, a limited feasibility study (directed March 1959 by Army R&D, assigned to Army Ordnance Missile Command) on establishing a manned US lunar outpost. Justifications: national space policy, demonstrating leadership, and supporting science, reconnaissance, communications, launch sites, and rescue. Notes rapid space advances (V-2, Sputnik, US/USSR satellites and probes), a planned first US manned lunar landing possibly by 1965, and scientific value of lunar experiments. Argues that failing to be first in space has damaged US prestige, and that the USSR may land on the moon by 1965 with political and military consequences.

nodes.title: 6. Security Implications
nodes.summary: Argues that a US lunar outpost is a security and political priority: being first gives the option to choose peaceful or military use and creates a proprietary-like claim, while other space applications (reconnaissance, meteorology, communications) show interest but carry less impact. Concludes that Project HORIZON is the earliest feasible route, with an operational outpost by late 1966 and initial manned landings in spring 1965, and that early decision and adequate funding are imperative to avoid losing a race with the USSR.

nodes.title: 7. Summa ry
nodes.summary: Argues it is imperative for the US to establish a lunar outpost early, since being first confers political and proprietary-like standing, and that other space applications (reconnaissance, meteorology, communications) show interest but lack the same impact. Concludes Project HORIZON is the earliest feasible route (operational outpost by late 1966, initial manned landings Spring 1965), that delay raises cost and lowers reliability, and that the Army can contribute across the program. Describes Volume I (summary, non-technical factors, Army resources) and Volume II (technical concepts, funding, personnel, space policy, legal issues), prepared by an ABMA working group with Army technical service representatives under a conservative engineering philosophy.

Project HORIZON, a limited 1959 Army feasibility study for a manned US lunar outpost, justified by space policy, leadership, science, reconnaissance, communications, and rescue, citing rapid space advances and a possible 1965 Soviet landing. Argues a US outpost is a security and political priority, since being first confers peaceful or military options and a proprietary-like claim. Concludes Project HORIZON is the earliest feasible route (outpost by late 1966, manned landings by spring 1965), that early decision and funding are imperative, and outlines Volumes I and II and the Army's role.

nodes.title: A. OBJECTIVES AND SCOPE OF THE STUDY
nodes.summary: Describes the study's objectives and scope for feasibility of expediting a lunar outpost establishment. It relates U.S. capabilities and developments to the task, covering design criteria for the lunar outpost, the Earth-Moon transportation system, communications systems, and Earth support facilities and operations. Technical assumptions on design parameters are realistic yet conservative, and assumptions about supporting U.S. programs (HORIZON) are reasonable and aligned with current and projected efforts.

nodes.title: B. RESUME OF THE TECHNICAL PROGRAM
nodes.summary: Project HORIZON outlines a lunar outpost program using SATURN I and II carrier vehicles. SATURN I is operational by October 1963; SATURN II development runs 1962-1964 with improved engines. By end-1964, 72 SATURN launches are expected (40 for HORIZON). Cargo deliveries begin January 1965, first two-man landing April 1965, and a 12-person outpost is manned November 1966. The buildup needs 61 SATURN I and 88 SATURN II launches (about 5.3 per month), delivering roughly 490,000 pounds of cargo. The first operational year (Dec 1966-1967) has 64 launches adding 266,000 pounds. Total cost is about $6 billion over 8.5 years (~$700 million/year), under two percent of the annual defense budget.

nodes.title: C. OUTPOST
C. OUTPOST (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes the proposed Project HORIZON lunar outpost: a permanent facility for 12 personnel, with its site yet to be chosen via exploratory probing and mapping (three candidate sites within ±20° of the moon's optical center; lunar mapping planned for 1960 and 1962). Design is driven by the lunar environment (no atmosphere, 1/6 gravity, shorter horizon, extreme temperature swings from +248°F to -202°F, subsurface -40°F at equator) and transport limits, and is deemed solvable with current technology.

nodes.title: 3. Outpost Facilities and Their Installation
nodes.summary: Describes a planned 1965 lunar outpost (HORIZON). Two men land in April 1965 to verify unmanned surveys and cargo at the site, living in their lunar vehicle. A nine-man construction crew arrives July 1965, growing to 12, with camp operational within 15 days. Facilities are buried double-walled vacuum-insulated 10-ft by 20-ft tanks at about -40F, powered by nuclear reactors, with cargo containers for storage, surface construction and transport vehicles, and a parabolic antenna for earth communication. The completed 12-man outpost adds power supplies, cold storage, and labs. Gas supply is from insulated liquid oxygen and nitrogen tanks, with CO2 and moisture control by chemical absorbent, later a CO2 freeze-out system.

nodes.title: 4. Personnel Equipment
nodes.summary: Explains that a sustained lunar-surface operation needs a body-conformation suit with a substantial outer metal surface, for reasons including pressure-leakage uncertainty, meteoroid protection, reflectivity, abrasion durability, and cleaning/sterilization. Notes suit earth-weight can be substantial (300 lb on Earth is 50 lb on the Moon). Describes planned special tools, load-handling gear, and dining equipment; food starts pre-cooked, moving to dehydrated/frozen as water reclamation grows, with hydroponic salads and closed-cycle food systems to be developed.

nodes.title: D . SPACE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM
1. Flight Mechanics
nodes.summary: Describes Project HORIZON's flight mechanics: trajectory tradeoffs between low-energy paths (max payload, sensitive, long transit) and high-energy paths (faster, robust, payload penalties, higher braking). Target earth-to-moon transit is about 50-60 hours. Covers four trajectory types (direct earth-moon, earth to 96-minute orbit, orbit to moon, moon to earth). Compares direct landing versus orbital-staging schemes: direct needs a 12-million-pound thrust six-stage vehicle, while orbital uses two-million-pound vehicles with refueling and gives about ten times the payload. Orbital approach is mandatory for the schedule. Earth return uses aerodynamic braking with a Jupiter-nose-cone-like body, supported by a primate test flight.

nodes.title: 2. Orbital Carrier and Space Vehicles
nodes.summary: Project HORIZON uses two carrier vehicles: SATURN I (clustered booster, 1,504,000 lb lift-off thrust, second and LOX/hydrogen third stages; 30,000 lb to 96-min orbit, 1,500 lb to escape) and SATURN II (upgraded booster to 2,000,000 lb thrust with H-2 engines; 70,000 lb to orbit, 26,750 lb to escape). Cargo can be soft-landed on the moon directly (6,000 lb) or via earth orbit with propellant transfer (48,000 lb), which also supports personnel. Lunar landing vehicles and a 10-16 man orbital return vehicle are described.

nodes.title: 3. Guidance a11-d Control
nodes.summary: Project HORIZON guidance: known hardware and techniques suffice. Final injection velocity uses conventional control; mid-course guidance brings the lunar vehicle within about 20 km of target; target-oriented terminal guidance reduces landing error (3-sigma) to about 1.5 km. Transportation: by end of 1967, about 252 persons reach earth orbit, 42 go to the moon, 26 return; orbital station crew of about ten rotates every few months. About 756,000 lb of cargo delivered to the lunar surface, requiring 229 SATURN firings, reduced to 73 boosters via recovery.

Project HORIZON's space transportation system: flight mechanics compare low-energy (max payload, slow ~50-60 hr earth-moon transit) and high-energy trajectories; direct landing needs a 12M-lb six-stage vehicle while orbital staging with refueling uses 2M-lb vehicles and gives ~10x payload, and is mandatory for schedule; earth return uses aerodynamic braking, supported by a primate test flight. Carriers: SATURN I (30,000 lb to orbit) and SATURN II (70,000 lb to orbit); cargo delivery by direct soft landing (6,000 lb) or via earth orbit with propellant transfer (48,000 lb); lunar landing and 10-16 man return vehicles. Guidance uses known hardware; terminal guidance cuts landing error to ~1.5 km. Traffic projections by 1967: ~252 to earth orbit, 42 to moon, 26 returned; ~756,000 lb cargo to lunar surface, reduced from 229 to 73 boosters via recovery.

nodes.title: F. COMMUNICATIONS ELECTRONICS
nodes.summary: Describes Project HORIZON's communications: an earth-based and lunar-based complex, each with communications and surveillance functions, including a 24-hour equatorial communications satellite and a world-wide surveillance net expandable with two 85-foot antennas. Covers lunar surface communications (helmet radios, relay stations, TV, photos, homing, emergency packs, infrared and radar detectors). Also covers launch vehicle requirements/schedules, and a survey finding Atlantic and Pacific Missile Ranges unsuitable, leading to a new equatorial launch site with eight pads, with Brazil assumed.

nodes.title: H. PROGRAM LOGISTICS
I. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
I. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT (intro)
I. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT (intro)
nodes.summary: Covers Project HORIZON's program logistics, which find military participation in logistic support mandatory (level undetermined given world politics), and its research and development plan. Six phases are outlined: Phase I feasibility study completed 9 June 1959; Phase II detailed development and funding plan (about eight months, $5.4 million); Phase III hardware development and system integration across systems, subsystems, components, and procedures; Phase IV lunar outpost construction; Phase V outpost operations from December 1966; Phase VI expansion from January 1968. Also covers basic research areas (life support, space medicine, lunar systems, power, materials) and the development program.

nodes.title: Project HORIZON Lunar Outpost Phases and Supporting Research
nodes.summary: Describes program Phases IV-VI: Phase IV builds the lunar outpost using Phase II systems, fulfilling the goal to establish a manned lunar outpost; Phase V begins outpost operations in December 1964 as the first fully operational phase; Phase VI expansion is assumed to start January 1968. Covers basic and supporting research needs (food, oxygen, clothing, bio-medical, vacuum, weightlessness, meteoroids, lunar systems, mapping, explosives, power, materials, liquid hydrogen, lunar soil mechanics). Explains Project HORIZON development: Phase I completed, Phase II must proceed on schedule, its plan details Phase III development work and later requirements.

nodes.title: 3. Research and Development Facilities
nodes.summary: Describes HORIZON's research and development facilities: a large lunar environmental simulator for research, development, testing and training for HORIZON and other national space projects; a space flight simulator for training and research on boost acceleration, coasting, weightlessness and braking deceleration; and a co-located medical research facility. Also includes the HORIZON research and development program timeline (1960-1968) with phases from initial feasibility study through expansion of initial capabilities, and figure references (I-21 to I-23) for the R&D organization, main facility cross-section and flight simulator.

Project HORIZON program logistics: military participation in logistic support is mandatory, level undetermined. Six-phase R&D plan: Phase I feasibility study completed 9 June 1959; Phase II detailed development and funding (about eight months, $5.4M); Phase III hardware development and system integration; Phase IV lunar outpost construction; Phase V outpost operations from December 1964 or 1966; Phase VI expansion from January 1968. Covers basic research (life support, space medicine, lunar systems, power, materials, food, oxygen, mapping, lunar soil) and facilities: a lunar environmental simulator, a space flight simulator for training, and a co-located medical research facility, with the 1960-1968 R&D timeline and figures I-21 to I-23.

nodes.title: A. SCOPE OF OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: Establishing a manned lunar outpost requires defining operational concepts and facilities to derive an organizational structure. A terrestrial launch site is needed because existing US sites are saturated with weapons R&D firings, have limited monthly firing windows, and lie far from the equator, which wastes energy. A site near the equator would ease orbital rendezvous and avoid the payload penalty and trajectory complexity of dog-legging from non-equatorial sites. Chapter V discusses these factors further.

nodes.title: c. Magnitude of effort requred to implement the objectives
3. Orbital Station
nodes.summary: Preliminary feasibility study on a lunar mission. Covers: effort needed to meet objectives; diplomatic, political, military vulnerability, and cost factors in site choice; an equatorial terrestrial launch site as the first lunar-landing site, needing immediate negotiation and early build-up, also supporting other military and NASA projects. Orbital station: chosen over direct launch for energy and emergency return; austere early phase using vehicle shells, later upgraded to several stations with tankage. Listed benefits include labs, storage, relay, surveillance, meteorology, geodesy, and weapons-effects instrumentation, and eventual independent agency. Lunar outpost: first 30-90 day phase focuses on life support and human verification of prior probe data.

nodes.title: Space Station Support Roles and Early Lunar Outpost Life Support
key_items: a. Life Support and Preliminary Exploration.
nodes.summary: Lists potential contributions of an advanced orbital station: space laboratory, training, materiel storage, low-altitude communication relay, Earth, space, and meteorological surveillance, geodesy data collection, and weapon-effects instrumentation. Station may evolve into an independent agency. Introduces the lunar outpost goal, whose first 30-90 day phase focuses on life support and human verification of prior unmanned data, informing permanent site selection.

nodes.title: Project HORIZON: Lunar Outpost Construction and Initial Operational Capability
key_items: c. Benefical Occupancy and Initial Operational Capability
nodes.summary: Second outpost phase uses personnel and cargo near the permanent site to build habitable structures, with roughly 18-month rotations (maximum one-year tours) under a construction-specialist head. The goal is beneficial occupancy supporting 12 people, six mainly on maintenance and life support. Later expansion adds equipment, lunar launch use, and early industrialized self-regeneration from returned samples.

nodes.title: B. ORGANIZATIONAL AND OPERATIONAL CONCEPTS
nodes.summary: B. ORGANIZATIONAL AND OPERATIONAL CONCEPTS

nodes.title: 1. General
nodes.summary: Discusses the lunar outpost's launch site and orbital station supporting R&D and operations, requiring military (air/sea transport), NASA scientific, and logistics support that overlaps existing unified commands. Cross-government coordination is needed with the NSC, CIA, State Department, FBI, Coast and Geodetic Survey, USGS, and AEC. Site requirements may raise diplomatic issues, including land leases (e.g., Panama Canal Zone model) or purchase, affecting organization and needing further study.

nodes.title: 2. Over-all Management Structure
nodes.summary: Describes project management requirements for a space program: overall authority to direct operations from U.S. support through launch site, orbital station, and lunar outpost; sufficient organizational depth; day-to-day liaison with military and civil government departments; and need for a U.S.-based project management agency. Subordinate co-equal activities include the terrestrial launch site, fully operational orbital station, lunar outpost, training agencies, specialized technical support (communications and tracking), and possible field offices at transport terminals, depots, and R&D sites. Each agency has mission duties to management and peers, some with special delegated authorities. Launch site and management need conventional and space-peculiar technical support with cross-service capability; technical channels prevail without diluting responsibility.

nodes.title: 3. Staff Organization
nodes.summary: Staffing of an orbital station and lunar outpost requires diverse carefully selected skills, with early activation, staffing, and training of agencies being mandatory to avoid operational delays. National security sees being first on the lunar surface as critical for political and psychological reasons, since being second is unacceptable. Policy guidance is general and undeveloped; no specific policy for this venture exists, requiring future development, correlation, and codification, judged against contemporary international political and military situations.

nodes.title: Non-Technical Considerations: National Security Importance of Lunar Outpost First
key_items: CHAPTER IV: NON- TECHNICAL SUPPORTING CONSIDERATIONS
nodes.summary: Chapter IV, General section. From a national security viewpoint, establishing a lunar outpost makes being first essential, preserving the option between peaceful and military uses. Being first carries major political and psychological significance, with being second considered intolerable given past space accomplishments.

nodes.title: B. POLICY
nodes.summary: Describes policy guidance for a major space study: policy is still general and evolving, with no specific policy found for this subject; an existing-policy summary is in Appendix A, and early codification is needed. Policy must be judged against contemporary international political and military context, and the urgency is clear. Intelligence estimates credit the Soviet Union with the capability to accomplish the study's objectives after 1965, implying a national policy requirement. Section C on political, psychological, and security implications is referenced but not included.

nodes.title: 1. Political and Psychological
nodes.summary: Argues that failing to be first in space, especially to land a man on the Moon, would carry serious political and psychological costs, lowering US military, scientific, and political prestige. The Soviets openly aim for a lunar landing, possibly by 1967, and the precedent would have legal implications. Other space applications could yield military capabilities sooner but lack the same impact. A lunar outpost is the most immediate step and a basis for further exploration. Legal and policy details are in Appendices A and B.

nodes.title: 2. National Security
nodes.summary: Describes a national security section of a lunar study: a twelve-man outpost with six men handling life support, with further military applications depending on evaluations beyond the study's scope. Lists seven evaluation areas: threats to the outpost and counter-policy, significance of lunar operations for national defense, military requirements for National Security Council policies, implementation costs, use of knowledge from early phases, national policy goals for capabilities, and rocket booster engine improvements.

Later phases add construction (12-person capacity, ~18-month rotations), industrialized self-regeneration, and inter-agency coordination (NSC, CIA, State, FBI, USGS, AEC). Management needs unified authority and a US project agency. Staffing and early activation are critical. Being first is a national security priority; policy is undeveloped. nodes.title: APPEND!?{ A: POLICY OF THE UNITED STATES WITH RESPECT TO ACTIVITIES IN SPACE
1, Statements by the President of the United States
nodes.summary: A 1959-era U.S. policy excerpt quoting President Eisenhower on space activities: the January 1959 State of the Union and Budget messages cite five satellites placed in orbit, NASA's 1958 scientific satellite and probe programs, weather and communications satellites, and high-energy and nuclear rocket development. An April 1958 message to Congress lists four factors urging space advancement (human curiosity, military potential, national prestige, scientific knowledge), recommends a civilian space agency with military projects left to the Defense Department.

nodes.title: 2. Policy Declarations by the Congress

a. Senate Report Number 1?01, dated .11 June 1958, and House Report Number 1770, dated 24 Mayl958J and Conference Report Number 2166_, dated 15 July 1958, dealing with the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 (HR 12575), stated in pertinent part:
nodes.summary: Excerpts from 1958 U.S. Congressional reports on the National Aeronautics and Space Act: space exploration is framed as a sustained, long-range national effort, not a reaction to Soviet successes. It stresses the military and deterrent value of space, satellite reconnaissance and communications, and the need to leapfrog Soviet achievements through national mobilization. It contrasts the Soviet centralized astronautics agency (the Academy of Sciences, 1955) with the fragmented U.S. effort and urges one coordinated national plan. It concludes that entering the space age is urgent for national survival.

nodes.title: b. HR No. 1758, 85th Congress, Second Session, dated 2.1 May 1958, stated in relevant part:
nodes.summary: Excerpt of House Report No. 1758 (85th Congress, 1958) arguing that a national civilian space agency is urgent for defense and peaceful use, with control in civilian hands under the President and the agency head as supreme arbiter of astronautics policy, subject to National Security Council deliberation. It requires binding coordination with the Department of Defense and ARPA, which should keep primarily military projects but not monopolize space decisions. It notes the USSR leads, that large satellites, lunar and planetary probes, and crewed spaceflight are coming, that space development will pay large economic dividends, and that national survival requires entering the space age for peaceful benefit to all mankind.

nodes.title: c. The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958, Public Law 85-568, declared the policy and purposes of Congress in the following message:
nodes.summary: Excerpt from the National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 (Public Law 85-568), Section 102. It declares U.S. space policy that activities in space be devoted to peaceful purposes for all mankind. It states that aeronautical and space activities are required for general welfare and security, and assigns their direction to a civilian agency, except for military, weapons, and defense-related activities, which fall under the Department of Defense. The President decides which agency has responsibility per section 201(e).

nodes.summary: Excerpt from a 1959 House Select Committee report on astronautics and space exploration (HR 2710, 85th Congress). It argues the free world's survival depends on a bold space program, notes space technology serves both war and peace, and says the US backs peaceful space use at the UN. It warns military space capabilities are inseparable from peaceful ones (reconnaissance, mapping, communications, rockets, satellites). It also states the Soviet Union already runs a massive, high-priority space program and believes it will lead.

title: APPENDIX B: LEGAL AND POLITICAL IMPLICATIONS

nodes.title: APPENDIX B: LEGAL AND POLITICAL IMPLICATIONS (intro)
nodes.summary: Argues there is no established space law: international law is largely aspirational for outer space and the lunar surface, and treaties like the UN Charter are hard to interpret or enforce. Precedents from discovery and occupation are inconclusive, and force may decide control. Land disputes are usually political, not judicial. US Antarctic policy, set by Secretary Hughes in 1924, requires actual settlement or occupation for sovereignty claims, and the US reserves its rights without claiming territory. By analogy, the US needs continuous practical activity, such as an operating lunar base, to have standing in lunar affairs.

nodes.title: 3, THE LAW OF SPACE
3, THE LAW OF SPACE (intro)
nodes.summary: Discusses the law of space in relation to Project HORIZON: no binding precedents exist, so the proposed activities violate no settled international law, and the US has no legal obligations for outer space activity except regarding war waged from space. Notes the Island of Palmas principle on sovereignty. Argues law should await practical needs rather than premature rules, and warns the USSR uses law selectively and will bind the US to rules if it adopts them. Soviet scholars Korovin (reconnaissance satellites not acts of war; shooting down satellites may be) and Zadorozhynyi (satellites don't violate sovereignty) are cited but not authoritative state positions. Concludes outer space is open to all nations, not ownable, with sovereignty not extending beyond atmosphere; space law should develop as a flexible web of arrangements.

nodes.title: 4. POLITICAL IMPLICATIONS
nodes.summary: Argues that a nation's first duty is durability and that force is the ultimate sanction of law, citing Spengler and Justice Holmes on power struggles. Notes US and Soviet preeminence and the Soviet 'peaceful coexistence' strategy. Outlines US space policy: security first, civilian scientific control, military capabilities in space, and the 1958 Space Act's urgency. Concludes that Project HORIZON is required for national survival.

Within the law-of-space section (Project HORIZON), no binding precedents exist, so proposed activities violate no settled law; the US has no outer-space obligations except war waged from space. Sovereignty per the Island of Palmas principle; law should await practical need. Soviet scholars Korovin and Zadorozhynyi are cited (satellite reconnaissance, shootdown, sovereignty) but are not official positions. Outer space is open to all, not ownable, and sovereignty ends at the atmosphere; law should be a flexible web. Political section: national durability comes first, force backs law (Spengler, Holmes), Soviet 'peaceful coexistence', US space policy (security, civilian control, military space, 1958 Space Act), so HORIZON is needed for survival.

nodes.title: S. SPECIFIC PROBLEMS
S. SPECIFIC PROBLEMS (intro)
nodes.summary:
S. SPECIFIC PROBLEMS
The following specific problems have been submitted by members , o f the commi ttee on the Army Study for Establishment oi a Lunar - Outpost for legal analysis:

nodes.title: Problem 1:
nodes.summary: Analyzes hypothetical Russian lunar claims against a U.S. moon program. Covers (a) hard-landing a vehicle with a USSR flag/monument to claim the lunar surface, (b) soft-landing with flag, monument, radio or light, (c) same with men aboard, and (d) same plus a threat to destroy aggressors. Opinion: flags, landings, or symbolic acts do not confer territorial title under international law, since symbolic occupation is unrecognized; only actual settlement or occupation counts, as with Antarctica. Under threat (d), doing nothing could create a new lunar law principle, so resisting it becomes a political decision settled by force.

nodes.title: Problem 2.:
nodes.summary: Covers a hypothetical where Russians land on the moon first and claim a roughly 2000 sq mile lunar area. Reasonableness of the area is not the determinant; effective occupation (possession or actual settlement) is required. Settlement on an area's fringe would not vest rights beyond the actually occupied area. Disputes over control areas are political questions resolved by political branches, not courts, and may require national strength or war.

nodes.title: Problems 3 and 4 :
nodes.summary: Covers Problems 3 and 4 on lunar resource claims: whether arriving first (US or USSR) gives a right to claim a valuable resource concentration, how trespass by the other side should be handled, and whether a rival's claim would be ignored. The opinion holds that discovery plus claiming possession is insignificant once effective occupation ends, as with the US position on Antarctica, though that is not binding for lunar activity. Actual possession should be respected. Trespass implies more than peaceful entry, and courts are unlikely to resolve such disputes, so the outcome would be diplomatic or political negotiation, or war in the worst case.

nodes.title: Problem 5 :
nodes.summary: Hypothetical cold-war lunar scenario: US and USSR occupy separate moon sectors. Covers capture and detention of a US vehicle or personnel by the Russians (political, not judicial, resolution; outcomes unpredictable); a duty to protect other states from injurious acts by individuals; the right of entry for aircraft in distress (force majeure, Lissitzyn); limits on force, which must be necessary and proportionate to threat; no right to destroy unidentified vehicles without an established threat; mere territorial claims need not be recognized; ground intrusion and interference with supply vehicles lack legal basis in space, a common area, so resolution is political.

nodes.title: Problem 6:
nodes.summary: The text discusses a hypothetical in which a U.S. lunar return vehicle accidentally lands in the USSR, which withholds information and personnel. It notes international law recognizes innocent passage and that such a vehicle should be returned to its originating state, but no tribunal can enforce this, so only political or diplomatic action is available, with uncertain outcomes given Soviet relations. It concludes that rights and duties in space are uncertain, experience matters more than logic, and America should pursue its practical objectives without hindrance from general or international law.

Analyzes hypothetical lunar claims by Russia against a U.S. moon program: flag or monument landings do not confer title; only effective occupation or settlement does, as with Antarctica. Covers claims to a 2000 sq mile area, resource-site trespass, cold-war sector capture and detention, limits on force, aircraft in distress, and a vehicle landing in the USSR. Disputes are political, not judicial, and may end in negotiation or war. Space rights remain uncertain.

summary: Argues international space law is largely aspirational and untested: treaties are hard to enforce, discovery and occupation precedents are inconclusive, and force may decide control. US Antarctic policy (Hughes, 1924) requires actual settlement or occupation for sovereignty, so the US needs an operating lunar base to have standing. Within the law-of-space section (Project HORIZON), no binding precedents exist; outer space is open to all, not ownable, and sovereignty ends at the atmosphere. Political section stresses national durability, force backing law, Soviet coexistence, and US space policy. Hypothetical Russian lunar claims analyzed: flags do not confer title, only effective occupation does; disputes are political and may end in war.

title: APPENDIX C: TECHNICAL SERVICES SUPPORT CAPABILITIES
summary: Appendix C describes the U.S. Army's seven Technical Services (Ordnance, Engineers, Signal, Quartermaster, Chemical, Transportation, Medical) and their support for space exploration. They own about $1 billion in R&D facilities, employ roughly 40,000 personnel, and spend over $400 million yearly, supplemented by about $3/4 billion from industry. R&D covers four areas: missile and space systems, human performance in any environment, electronics, and construction/mapping/engineering materials. The Services conduct much of the nation's missile and space work for the Army, other services, ARPA, and NASA.

title: RESOURCES AND CAPABILITIES

nodes.title: RESOURCES AND CAPABILITIES (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Army Ordnance R&D resources: DOFL's micro-miniaturization and proximity fuze work, Picatinny's atomic munitions and climatic test facilities, Detroit's terradynamics and vehicle testing, Watertown's metals research and reactor, and AOMC's missile management with ABMA, ARGMA, and White Sands Missile Range. Includes a 1955-1960 table of R&D skills, facilities dollar values, personnel, and out-of-house support by category, and AOMC's role in Project HORIZON.

nodes.title: Engineers
nodes.summary: The Corps of Engineers supports the national space and missile program and runs Army engineering, construction, and real estate services. Its main research labs include USAERDL (about 1300 staff, Fort Belvoir), the Waterways Experiment Station (hydraulics, concrete, soils, pavement), the Army Nuclear Power Program (nuclear plants, NPFO, Idaho reactor area), and SIPRE (snow, ice, permafrost research, about 102 specialists). Also covered are ACFEL (Arctic construction, 45 staff), the Rigid Pavement Laboratory (airfield pavements, Sharonville track), and the Marine Division (floating plants), plus 14 smaller testing labs. Personnel and budget tables for 1955-1960 and FY1959 out-of-house R&D support are included, along with the Army Map Service (about 3500 staff) and the Corps' scale as the world's largest construction agency.

nodes.title: Signal
nodes.summary: Describes the Signal Corps' over forty years of research and development in communications, components, electron devices, atmospheric research, radar, and electronics. It covers the Signal Corps R&D Laboratory at Fort Monmouth, New Jersey, a principal electronic research center. About 3,500 military and civilian scientists and support staff work there across more than 30 fields, including 698 Bachelor's, 109 Master's, 453 Doctoral holders, and 135 partial-degree students.

summary: Describes Army Ordnance R&D resources: DOFL micro-miniaturization and proximity fuzes, Picatinny atomic munitions and climatic testing, Detroit terradynamics, Watertown metals and reactor, AOMC missile management (ABMA, ARGMA, White Sands, Project HORIZON), with 1955-1960 R&D data. Corps of Engineers labs (USAERDL, Waterways Experiment Station, nuclear power, SIPRE, ACFEL, pavement, Marine Division) and Army Map Service. Signal Corps R&D Laboratory at Fort Monmouth, about 3,500 scientists and staff across 30+ fields.

title: ANALYSIS of USAS~tDL CIVILIAN PERSONNEL
summary: A 1959-era U.S. Army Signal Research and Development Laboratory overview covering civilian personnel statistics and facilities by technical division, contractual R&D spending (FY54-59), and the Electronic Defense Laboratory at Sylvania. It describes Signal Corps size, budget, and operations (communications, Signal Supply Agency, Electronics Proving Ground, White Sands, Pictorial Center). It also covers Army Medical Service research units and budgets, Quartermaster Corps research, depots, and clothing contracts, Transportation Corps R&D and resources, and Chemical Corps programs, facilities, personnel, and funding data.

title: CONCLUSIONS
summary: The Army Technical Services' research and development skills and resources form a substantial part of what Project HORIZON requires. These capabilities exist today and have demonstrated value to national programs. A more comprehensive discussion is in the publication "U.S. Army Capabilities in the Space Age." The remaining text is OCR noise and a document order stamp, with no further content.
